Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Latin word

dēbeō

dēbeō, dēbēre, dēbuī, dēbitum

verb, second conjugation, with an infinitive

ought, be bound to (a duty); owe; in the passive, be owed, be due; owe (money, thanks)

In this lexicon

  • be supposed to

    also used · classical · Petr. 45.1: nōn dēbēmus dēlicātī esse; Plin. Ep. 8.16.5: plūra fortasse quam dēbuī

  • due

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Att. 14.18.1: Kal. Jān. dēbuit, adhūc nōn solvit; Cic. Fam. 3.5.4: pecūnia … quae mihi ex pūblicā permūtātiōne dēbētur

  • owe

    the recommended word · classical · Mart. 2.3.1: Sexte, nihil dēbēs; Vulg. Lc. 16.5: quantum dēbēs dominō meō?

  • should

    also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 28.1: animum dēbēs mūtāre, nōn caelum; Cic. Sen. 69: eō dēbet esse contentus

Notes

  1. 1With an infinitive, dēbeō speaks of a duty, never of what is merely expected to happen: Lewis & Short, in classical prose always of moral necessity. Ruling: dēbeō is for duty.
  2. 2With an infinitive dēbeō speaks of a duty; for what simply has to be, Latin says necesse est. Lewis & Short: in classical prose always of moral necessity. Ruling: dēbeō is for duty.

Examples

  • Kal. Jān. dēbuit, adhūc nōn solvit

    the money was due on the first of January, and he still hasn’t paidCic. Att. 14.18.1

    In the entry for due

  • quam ad diem eī legiōnī quae in praesidiō relinquēbātur dēbērī frūmentum sciēbat

    the day on which, as he knew, corn was due to the legion left on guardCaes. BG 6.33.4

    In the entry for due

  • Sexte, nihil dēbēs, nīl dēbēs, Sexte, fatēmur: dēbet enim, sī quis solvere, Sexte, potest.

    You owe nothing, Sextus, nothing at all, Sextus, we admit it: for only a man who can pay owes anything, Sextus.Mart. 2.3

    In the entry for owe

  • quantum dēbēs dominō meō? at ille dīxit: centum cadōs oleī.

    How much do you owe my master? And he said: A hundred jars of oil.Vulg. Lc. 16.5–6

    In the entry for owe

  • Aesōpī nōmen sīcubi interposuerō, cui reddidī jam prīdem quicquid dēbuī, auctōritātis esse scītō grātiā

    If I bring in Aesop’s name anywhere, though I paid him long ago all I owed him, know that it is for the sake of his authorityPhaedr. 5 prol. 1–3

    In the entry for owe
